questions.q: The number of real solutions $x$ of the equation $\cos^{2}\left(xsin\left(2x\right)\right) + \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}} = \cos^{2}x + \sec^{2}x$ is
questions.solution:
We have,

$\cos^{2}\left(xsin\left(2x\right)\right) + \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}} = \cos^{2}x + \sec^{2}x$

$LHS = \cos^{2}\left(xsin2x\right) + \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}$

$\cos^{2}\left(xsin2x\right) + \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}} \le 2$

$RHS = \cos^{2}x + \sec^{2}x \ge 2$

$LHS = RHS$

$∴ \cos^{2}x + \sec^{2}x = 2$ at $x = 0$

Hence, only one solution.

questions.q: The number of solutions to $sin\left(\pi\sin^{2}\theta\right) + sin \left(\pi\cos^{2}\theta\right) =2cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}}}{2}cos\theta\right) satisfying $0 $\le \theta \lle2\pi$ is
questions.solution:
The given equation 

$sin\left(\pi{sin}^{2}\theta\right) + sin\left(\pi{cos}^{2}\theta\right) = 2cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}cos\theta\right)$

$⇒ 2sin\left(\dfrac{\pi\left({sin}^{2}\theta + {cos}^{2}\theta\right)}{2}\right)$

$cos\left(\dfrac{\pi\left({sin}^{2}\theta - {cos}^{2}\theta\right)}{2}\right) = 2cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}cos\theta\right)$

$⇒ cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}cos2\theta\right) = cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}cos\theta\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{\pi}{2}cos2\theta = 2n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{2}cos\theta$, $n \in$ Integers

$⇒ cos2\theta = 4n \pm cos\theta, n \in I$.

Case $I$

If $cos2\theta = 4n + cos\theta ⇒ cos2\theta - cos\theta = 4n$

The above equation will hold only if $n = 0$, 

so $cos2\theta = cos\theta$

$⇒ 2{cos}^{2}\theta - cos\theta - 1 = 0 ⇒ cos\theta = 1, - \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \theta = 2k\pi, 2k\pi \pm \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, k \in I$

$∵ \theta \in \left[0, 2\pi\right]$

So, $\theta = 0, 2\pi, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$

Case $II$

If $cos2\theta = 4n - cos\theta$

$⇒ cos2\theta + cos\theta = 4n$

The above equation will hold only if $n = 0$,

so $cos2\theta + cos\theta = 0$

$⇒ 2{cos}^{2}\theta + cos\theta - 1 = 0$

$⇒ cos\theta = - 1, \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \theta = \left(2m + 1\right)\pi, 2m\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3}, m \in I$.

$∵ \theta \in \left[0, 2\pi\right]$

So, $\theta = \pi, \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$

$∴$ There are total $7$ solutions.

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{9}{sin}^{2}\theta + \dfrac{4}{9}{cos}^{2}\theta + \dfrac{4}{9}sin\thetacos\theta$

$= \dfrac{1}{3}{sin}^{2}\theta + \dfrac{2}{3}{cos}^{2}\theta$

$⇒ \dfrac{2}{9}{sin}^{2}\theta + \dfrac{2}{9}{cos}^{2}\theta - \dfrac{4}{9}sin\thetacos\theta = 0$

$⇒ {sin}^{2}\theta + {cos}^{2}\theta - 2sin\thetacos\theta = 0$

$⇒ sin2\theta = 1$

questions.solution: $\begin{array}{l}\sin x+\frac{1}{2} \cos x=\sin ^{2}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ \sin x+\frac{1}{2} \cos x=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2}+2 x\right)\right. \\ \sin x+\frac{1}{2} \cos x=\frac{1}{2}(1+\sin 2 x) \\ 2 \sin x+\cos x=1+\sin x \cos x \\ 2 \sin x \cos x-2 \sin x+1-\cos x=0 \\ (1-\cos x)-2 \sin x(1-\cos x)=0 \\ (1-\cos x)(1-2 \sin x)=0 \\ 1-\cos x=0 & 1-2 \sin x=0 \\ \cos x=1 \quad \sin x=\frac{1}{2} \\ x=0, \quad x=\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{5 \pi}{6} \\ \text{ sum }=0+\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{5 \pi}{6}=\pi\end{array}$
